sources.source: Kimball Group, "Type 0: Retain Original" / "Type 1: Overwrite" / "Type 3: Add New Attribute"

items.item: Type 0: the value never changes, so facts are always grouped by it; appropriate for original-labeled attributes, durable identifiers, most date-dimension attributes

at.step: Reveal: Type 0, quoted directly

items.item: Type 1: the old value is overwritten with the new one, destroying history; easy to implement, no new rows, but aggregates and cubes must be recomputed

at.step: Reveal: Type 1, quoted directly

items.item: Type 3: adds a new attribute to preserve the old value (an "alternate reality"), while the main attribute is overwritten like Type 1; used relatively infrequently

at.step: Reveal: Type 3, quoted directly

sources.source: Kimball Group, "Type 4: Add Mini-Dimension" / "Type 5: Add Mini-Dimension and Type 1 Outrigger"

items.item: Type 4: a rapidly changing attribute group ("rapidly changing monster dimension") is split off into a mini-dimension with its own primary key; both base and mini-dimension keys go in the fact table

at.step: Reveal: Type 4, quoted directly — the mini-dimension, counted

items.item: Type 5: builds on Type 4 by embedding a current Type 1 reference in the base dimension, reading current mini-dimension attributes without a fact-table join; logically one presentation-layer table

at.step: Reveal: Type 5, quoted directly — current without a fact join

sources.source: Kimball Group, "Type 6: Add Type 1 Attributes to Type 2 Dimension" / "Type 7: Dual Type 1 and Type 2 Dimensions" / Design Tip #152

items.item: Type 6: Type 2 plus current Type 1 versions of the same attributes, overwritten on every row for the durable key whenever the value updates

at.step: Reveal: Type 6 and Type 7, quoted directly — the update cost, counted

items.item: Type 7: dual keys (surrogate for Type 2, durable for current), delivering Type 6's functionality via two separate views instead of overwriting

at.step: Reveal: Type 6 and Type 7, quoted directly — the update cost, counted

items.item: The hybrid type numbers are arithmetic on the simpler types: Type 5 because 4 + 1 = 5; Type 6 because both 2 + 3 + 1 and 2 × 3 × 1 equal 6

at.step: Reveal: Type 5, quoted directly — current without a fact join

items.item: The first predict (step 4) is red-teamed against the plausible wrong answer that preserving an old value always requires a second row; the reveal shows Type 3 doing it with a second column on the same row instead

at.step: Predict: can one column hold both the current value and the original, without a new row?

items.item: The gallery (step 6) is a real counted comparison, not four separate hypotheticals: the same reclassification run through Types 0, 1, 2 and 3, counted by row and column, so the only real difference between them is made visible at a glance

at.step: Reveal: the gallery, one change, four treatments, counted

items.item: The second predict (step 7) is red-teamed against the plausible wrong answer that Type 2 scales the same regardless of what changes; the reveal distinguishes a single narrow attribute (Type 2's own case, reserved for the closing "Prove it") from a shared, grouped, rapidly changing attribute set, which is specifically what forces the wide-row duplication Type 4 exists to avoid

at.step: Predict: does a rapidly changing, shared attribute group force Type 2's cost onto the whole dimension?

items.item: The mini-dimension sizing (step 8) and the Type 6/7 update-cost contrast (step 11) are this topic's own disclosed, self-consistent worked scenario, computed and asserted in examples.py since this topic has no lab of its own (CHAPTER.md) — not a claim about a real running system, and marked as such in SOURCES.md and FACT-CHECK.md

items.item: The third predict (step 10) is red-teamed against the plausible wrong answer that two techniques delivering the identical report must cost the identical amount; the reveal separates write-time cost (rewriting history, or not) from read-time cost (one join style or two), which the two hybrids trade against each other

at.step: Predict: can Type 6 and Type 7 both deliver current-plus-historical reporting, at different cost?

items.item: The three scenarios in the choosing step are deliberately spread across the churn spectrum — never-changing, changed-but-worthless, and fast-changing-and-shared — rather than three variations of the same case, so the decision rule is shown doing real work three different ways

at.step: Reveal: choosing by churn and query pattern, applied to three scenarios

items.item: The recap keeps "keep it or not" (0/1/3), "split it off" (4), and "named combinations" (5/6/7) as three separate ideas, matching the three-part structure Design Tip #152 itself uses (the basic three, then Type 4, then the hybrids), rather than collapsing seven types into one vague "pick one" takeaway
